Why Lighthouses Still Matter in the Age of GPS

By Connor Halloran — April 18, 2025

On a foggy night off the coast of Maine, a lobster boat threads its way back to harbor. The captain has a chartplotter, a depth sounder, and AIS — yet his eyes are fixed on the slow, rhythmic sweep of light from a stone tower built more than a century ago. Lighthouses, it turns out, still matter. They are not relics. They are stubbornly useful, and the reasons cut against the easy narrative that GPS made them obsolete.

The case against lighthouses sounds simple. Every mariner carries multiple GPS receivers. Phones have satellite navigation. Vessels above a certain tonnage are required to carry ECDIS, the electronic chart system. With centimeter-level positioning available for free, why bother maintaining beacons whose only job is to say "you are near a rock"? The answer is that GPS fails — quietly, occasionally, and in exactly the conditions where you most need to know where you are.

Solar storms can degrade GPS for hours. Spoofing attacks, increasingly common in coastal regions near conflict zones, can shift a vessel's apparent position by miles. Multipath reflections in narrow harbors give jittery, unreliable fixes. And of course, batteries die, antennas fail, and software crashes at the worst possible moment. A lighthouse is indifferent to all of this. It works as long as the bulb is lit and the lens is clean.

Lighthouse beams are also distinctively timed. Each station has its own "character": Boon Island flashes white every five seconds; Cape Neddick alternates red and white at a specific cadence. A trained mariner can identify a station from its flash pattern alone, without consulting any chart. This is a fundamentally different kind of information than a GPS coordinate. It is local, embodied, and survives in the absence of digital systems. It is also, crucially, hard to spoof.

Beyond their practical role, lighthouses serve as fixed points in the cultural geography of the coast. They show up on tourist brochures and postcards because they actually mean something to the communities around them. Decommissioning a lighthouse is not like turning off a streetlight; it provokes letters to the editor and town hall meetings. The Coast Guard has learned, sometimes painfully, that the public reaction to shutting down a beacon outweighs the modest cost of keeping it lit.

There is a small but committed movement to modernize rather than mothball historic lighthouses. LED retrofits cut power draw to a fraction of the old incandescent bulbs. Remote monitoring eliminates the need for resident keepers. Solar panels and battery backups make outlying stations cost-effective. Several lighthouses on the East Coast have been converted to fully autonomous operation while preserving the original lens and structure. This is the kind of pragmatic preservation that actually keeps a system useful.

The international picture varies. France maintains an extensive network of beacons along its Atlantic coast and treats them as part of national heritage. Canada has been slower to automate but has begun a program of LED conversions. The United Kingdom's Trinity House manages a portfolio of around sixty active lighthouses, all now automated. The pattern is consistent: full closure is rare; automation is common; visible light, audible fog signals, and radar reflectors remain in service.

Perhaps the most surprising lesson is that lighthouses have never really been "just" navigation aids. They are a way for a coast to communicate with itself — to mark the transitions between land and sea, safety and danger, here and there. Pilots use them. Fishermen use them. Pleasure boaters use them. So do hikers walking the coastal trail, pointing at the tower in the distance and saying, "that's where we're headed." Wikipedia's lighthouse entry and the U.S. Lighthouse Society are good starting points if you want to read more.

So, will we still have lighthouses in fifty years? Almost certainly yes — fewer, perhaps, and quieter, but still there, still sweeping the dark. They are the cheapest insurance policy a maritime nation has, and they double as a low-bandwidth, tamper-resistant signal that no satellite constellation can match. In a world where infrastructure increasingly depends on stacks of invisible software, there is something deeply reassuring about a stone tower with a lamp on top.
